chapter_theme: The marutham decade of the wife against the bard: she bars the go-between and the man (37, 38, 46, 47), mocks the husband as a dancer worked by others (42), sets the son as her own against the bard's praise and against the man's use of the boy to gain entry (39, 41), weighs her age against his old promises (45, 48), and hears the other women's boasts and the town's gossip of his affair (40, 43, 44).

iraicchi.act: the buffalo in rut breaks away and plunges into the cool pond, scattering the men at work
iraicchi.sense: the man, hot with desire, goes heedless after his pleasures and leaves his household in an uproar

37.reading: The wife tells the bard of the man of the field town, where a buffalo in rut plunges with a splash into the cool pond and the ploughmen run from the uproar, to stop pouring out lies in front of her.
37.nuance: The two sound words pair the halves: the buffalo goes in தழென and the bard's lies come out பொழென, so the bard's rush of talk is heard as the same heedless plunge. As ullurai it is a near miss on condition 3: the buffalo's plunge maps onto the man's rush to other women, but the fleeing ploughmen have no clear partner in the love situation.

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo of the paddy fields and the ploughmen

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the wife refuses the bard who comes to plead for the man; the friend is possible as speaker

38.reading: The wife tells the man of the good town of paddy fields where shoals of carp leap that she has no liking left for him and he is not to come to her house from today, since he lives desiring the shoulders of young-breasted women; the last line is lost.
38.nuance: With line 4 lost, what he is to take (கொண்டு) or go to is gone; what survives is a door shut 'from today' (இன்றொடு), a dated break and not a passing sulk.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the wife refuses the man at her door

39.reading: The wife says the man of the river town, where the striped varaal fish feeds along the bank of the full old water and then leaps, comes to their house bringing his son in a garland of bound blossoms, pointing to the boy, only to torment them.
39.nuance: The son is his pass to the door, and she sees it: the garlanded child is shown (சுட்டி) to win entry, and she calls the visit harassment (அலைய), not a homecoming.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband seeking entry through the son

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the wife speaks of the man who comes with the son as his go-between

40.reading: Of the man of the fair field town where the tharaa ducks scatter, the street declares openly that he will come even though he does not; will these women like flowering creepers really get to join him?
40.nuance: The street (சேரி) is most likely the other women's quarter boasting of him; the speaker turns the boast into a question that doubts they will get him either, so his neglect is shared.

thinai_evidence.note: water birds of the paddy fields

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend scoffs at the other women's boast; the speaker and the women meant are uncertain

41.reading: The wife asks the bard what he gains by reciting the merits of the man of the good pond town: even without that she knows what he has done, and she has, as her own, a little son with a wet mouth whose babbling words are sweet.
41.nuance: அறிந்தோம் யாம் செய்தி can mean that she already knows his doings, or that she learned them from the boy's prattle; either way the son, not the bard's praise, is what she holds as hers (எனக்குடைமை).

comparisons.tenor: the husband, led about by others

42.reading: The wife asks the bard to whom he is telling the state and nature of the man of the flood-water town, and what she could do about it: if he is in want, let him take the man as his dancer, make him dance, and live on that.
42.nuance: The taunt reverses the roles: the bard, who dances for his meal, is told to make the husband the performer, as if the man already dances to others' tune.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulking against the bard of the man of the water town

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the wife mocks the bard who pleads for the man

43.reading: Women of pollen-shedding garlands who have no worth sulk at the man of the flower ford where lotus buds open, while other men's women stay silent and call him a stranger, taking the folly on themselves.
43.nuance: The verse sets two answers to his straying side by side: the open sulking of the women without standing and the silent estrangement of the wife who blames herself; which group the speaker counts herself in is the hard part.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the wife reflects on how women answer his straying; speaker uncertain

44.reading: The friend tells the woman of broad soft shoulders that the gossip picks out the man of the ford, saying he sought out a woman's bee-hummed garland, stayed with her and embraced her lovely breasts, and spreads it far and wide.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend reports the town's gossip about the man

45.reading: The wife tells the bard that they are old now, though young before, and that when the man of the cool rain-fed noisy fields hastened to them with many promising words of his goodness, they did not know he would one day leave them, as they know today.
45.nuance: Age is set against the earlier courtship: what she failed to foresee in youth (நீத்தல் அறிந்திலேம்) is what her ageing now lets her see.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the wife answers the bard who comes for the man

46.reading: The wife tells the useless lute-bard that the man of the good town of kaanchi trees, where water rushes into the ponds, spoke many pleasant things and seemed ashamed, so the bard should say nothing false and get up and go at once.
46.nuance: நாணினன் போன்றான் says he only looked ashamed: she treats his contrition as an act already seen through, which leaves the bard nothing to add.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanchi tree by the ponds

47.reading: The wife tells the lying bard of the man of the proud rich fields, where red water-lily, lotus, lovely red kazhuneer and massed valli creepers are thrust down amid the din, not to come into her house while she is there.
47.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe: whether the flowers are trampled, weeded out or pierced is unclear, so any hidden sense in the crushed flowers stays a guess and is not tagged.

48.reading: The wife tells the bard of the fitting lute that the man of the rich crane-filled fields does not embrace the lovely breasts heavy with cool sandal, and that they, grown old with sagging breasts, want him not to come seeking an answer.
48.nuance: Line 2 (பொலிவுடைத்தா) is unclear: it may be her irony on his 'splendid' conduct or the splendour of the breasts he passes over; the contrast of sandal-cool breasts and slack ones carries the poem either way.

links.note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the wife tells the bard to carry to the other women the man's description as lord of the town where the red-eyed buffalo breaks its clog, sinks into the pond and gorges on the crop. Kainnilai 37: the rutting buffalo plunges into the pond before the wife tells the bard to stop lying.
links.teaches: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49 tells the bard to deliver the buffalo as the man's own portrait, which shows that in Kainnilai 37 the same plunging buffalo set before the bard is a character sketch of the husband and not just the setting of his town.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 43: the woman tells the man his bard is a bigger liar than he is and swears many oaths. Kainnilai 37: the wife tells the bard to stop pouring out lies before her.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru 43 ranks the bard's lying above the man's, and Kainnilai 37 lets her silence the bard directly while the man is only named, so together they show the wife's anger moving onto the go-between as the safer target.

links.note: Kural 1311: the woman refuses the chest of the man she calls a philanderer, because all women feed on him with their eyes. Kainnilai 38: the wife bars him from her house from today because he lives desiring young women's shoulders.
links.teaches: The couplet's refusal rests on a witty pretext, that other women merely look at him, while the venba's rests on his actual desire for other women, so the pair shows the Kural turning a real grievance of the marutham poems into the fine point of a lovers' quarrel.

links.note: Natrinai 250: the man tells the bard how, coming near to hug his toddling son, his wife took it otherwise and shied away. Kainnilai 39: the wife says he comes bringing the garlanded son, pointing to him, to torment her. On the man's telling the son is a real tenderness she misreads; on hers it is a tactic.
links.teaches: Read together the two poems give both sides of the same approach through the child, the husband insisting his affection was misjudged and the wife calling it harassment, so neither poem's account can be taken as the plain fact of the scene.

links.note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50: the wife calls it folly that he seeks entry with the son as his backing. Kainnilai 39: he comes with the garlanded son, pointing to him, to trouble her.
links.teaches: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50 names the son as the man's 'witness' (துணைச்சான்றோன்) and Kainnilai 39 shows the boy dressed in a garland and pointed out, so the pair shows the child being staged as evidence of the marriage the husband has broken.

links.note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51: speaking of the man of the good pond town is my grief; get up and go, bard; I have my little son as companion. Kainnilai 41 opens with the same line (பொய்கைநல் லூரன் திறன்கிளப்ப) and ends with the little son as what she owns.
links.teaches: The two venbas share their first line and their closing son, but where Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51 calls the man's praise her grief (எவ்வம்), Kainnilai 41 says she already knows his doings, so the reworking turns the wife's pain into a cool dismissal while keeping the son as her answer.

links.note: Kalittokai 81: the wife asks the toddling son to repeat the words the 'mothers' of the big street taught him, and the husband blames the bard. Kainnilai 41: she knows his doings, having the sweet babbling son as her own.
links.teaches: Kalittokai 81 shows a son's prattle betraying where his father has taken him, which supports reading Kainnilai 41's 'we know' as knowledge gained from the boy's babble rather than only as a mother's comfort.

links.note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the wife tells the greasy-mouthed bard to go to the street of young women and eat there even if he must dance for it (கூத்தாடி உண்ணினும் உண்). Kainnilai 42: if he is in want, let the bard take the man as his dancer, make him dance and eat even so (ஆட்டுவித்து உண்ணினும் உண்).
links.teaches: The closing formula is the same, but Kainnilai moves the dancing from the bard to the husband, so the pair shows the later poet sharpening the taunt into a picture of the man as a performer worked by others.

links.note: Kainnilai 42: the bard may make the man his dancer. Kainnilai 46: the man spoke pleasantly and only seemed ashamed.
links.teaches: Verse 46 says his shame was a show and verse 42 makes him a dancer, so the decade presents the husband's contrition as performance from both sides, his own acting and the bard's staging.

links.note: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the son has been fed and we are old now (மூத்தேம் இனியாம்); go to the young women's street. Kainnilai 45: we are old now, bard (மூத்தேம் இனிப்பாண), young before, and we did not know he would leave.
links.teaches: Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47 offers age as the reason he goes to younger women, while Kainnilai 45 sets the same words against his old promises, so the pair shows the formula of the ageing wife used once to explain his straying and once to expose a betrayal she could not foresee.

links.note: Kainnilai 45: we are old now and did not know he would leave. Kainnilai 48: grown old with sagging breasts, we want no answer from him.
links.teaches: In 45 her age is the vantage from which she sees his promises were false, and in 48 it becomes the ground of her refusal, so the decade moves age from grief to a reason for closing the door.

links.note: Thinaimalai 131: the wife tells the graceless bard he need not fashion words to begin a reconciliation; she turned the day she heard the man's lies. Kainnilai 46: the man spoke many pleasant things and seemed ashamed; useless bard, say nothing false and go.
links.teaches: Thinaimalai 131 dates her refusal to the lies she heard, while Kainnilai 46 adds that the man had already acted out his shame, so the pair shows the bard's plea coming after the husband's own performance has failed.

links.note: Kuruntokai 127: because the man's one bard proved a liar, every bard looks like a thief to the women he left. Kainnilai 47: the wife calls the bard a liar (பொய்ப் பாண) and bars him from her house.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai 127 states the general effect of one lying go-between and Kainnilai 47 shows its consequence in a single house, the door shut to the bard himself, so the pair shows distrust of the messenger hardening into exclusion.

links.note: Natrinai 380: the friend refuses the bard, saying our breasts ooze milk, we smell of new birth and are no match for the man of the jewelled women's street. Kainnilai 48: the man does not embrace the sandal-cool breasts; we have grown old with sagging breasts; come for no answer.
links.teaches: Natrinai 380 makes motherhood the wife's disqualification and Kainnilai 48 makes age, so the pair shows the wife's body at two stages of marriage offered in the same mocking way as the reason the man has gone elsewhere.

source_issues: 37-48: the colophon gives only the thinai (மருதம்) and no thurai; every thurai_akam speech situation is inferred from the poem, with occasion words null.
38 line 4: the line is mostly lost (dots in the source); the verse is marked uncertain.
42 line 2: உரைத்திபாண runs உரைத்தி and பாண together.
45 line 2: ஊரான் stands where the decade elsewhere has ஊரன்; line 3 பாத்தில் பயமொழி is a rare phrase, read as 'words of promise'.
47 lines 1-2: ஒருக்கார்ந்த and ஒலித்தாரக் குத்தும் are hard to construe; the verse is marked uncertain.
48 line 2: பொலிவுடைத்தா is unclear; the verse is marked uncertain.
